text:
Behind an API, the data has to live somewhere, and usually that's a database. Its reads have to be fast, and its writes have to be right, even when another write lands at the same moment. Every number here comes from a run in Postgres, the open-source relational database, on a million users, a million orders, and a few small tables. Sixteen questions, plus one from system design. Eleven are worked through, and five go quickly at the end.

Question one. Sequel versus no-sequel, when do you pick each? And from system design: sequel or no-sequel at scale, how do you choose? Pick relational when the data is structured and its relationships matter: joins, transactions across several rows, strong consistency. It's the safe default for most applications. Pick no-sequel when writes must scale out across machines, when the schema keeps changing, which suits a document store, or when one access pattern, known in advance, runs at huge volume, which suits key-value or wide-column. The price: weaker consistency and limited joins. At scale, many systems use both: sequel for the core transactions, no-sequel for high-volume logs, sessions or feeds. So ask which queries you'll need next year. Relational answers a new one with a join; a store built around one access pattern may need the data copied again, arranged for the new one.
